[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"route_vs_seek","code":"/*
seek() points at the goal and pushes. That is correct and cheap when there is a straight line,
and when there is a barrier in the way it presses into the barrier for as long as you let it.
No amount of avoidWalls() fixes that: avoidance is local, and the decision to go the OTHER way
round a wall is not. route() plans — a radius-aware A* through the world's walls, smoothed
against the same swept test the physics uses, then followed waypoint by waypoint.

The maze is an S. The first barrier is open only at the BOTTOM, the second only at the TOP, so
no fixed "always turn left" solves it. Both arms run avoidWalls at the same weight: this is
routing against the best local steering available, not routing against nothing.
*/

val GOAL_X = 175.0
val GOAL_Y = 100.0
val STEPS = 1800 // 30 s at 60 Hz
val SEEDS = [1L, 2L, 3L, 4L]
val PER_SEED = 8

fun maze(seed: Long, routed: Boolean): ScriptWorld {
    val w = ScriptWorld(width = 200.0, height = 200.0, seed = seed, wrap = false)
    w.addWall(70.0, 45.0, 70.0, 200.0, name = "open at the bottom")
    w.addWall(130.0, 0.0, 130.0, 155.0, name = "open at the top")
    val jitter = kotlin.random.Random(seed) // same jitter in both arms: same start positions
    repeat(PER_SEED) {
        w.spawn(
            18.0 + jitter.nextDouble(-8.0, 8.0),
            100.0 + jitter.nextDouble(-28.0, 28.0),
            maxSpeed = 35.0,
            radius = 1.2,
            steerResponse = 0.3,
            tag = if (routed) "routed" else "direct",
        ) {
            val goal = point(GOAL_X, GOAL_Y) // R3c: this now works inside moveUntil too
            moveUntil(maxSeconds = STEPS / 60.0, speed = 35.0, until = { near(goal, 6.0) }) {
                if (routed) route(goal, clearance = 3.5) else seek(goal)
                avoidWalls(clearance = 3.0, weight = 0.6)
                separate(range = 4.0, weight = 0.4)
            }
            rest(2.0)
        }
    }
    return w
}

val curves = LinkedHashMap<String, List<Double>>()
val shown = LinkedHashMap<String, ScriptWorld>()
for (routed in [true, false]) {
    val name = if (routed) "routed" else "direct"
    val cumulative = MutableList(STEPS) { 0.0 }
    var population = 0
    var travel = 0.0
    for (s in SEEDS) {
        val w = maze(s, routed)
        val done = mutableSetOf<Int>()
        repeat(STEPS) { t ->
            w.step()
            for (a in w.actors) if (a.id !in done && a.distanceTo(GOAL_X, GOAL_Y) <= 6.0) done += a.id
            cumulative[t] = cumulative[t] + done.size
        }
        population += w.actors.size
        travel += w.totalPathLength()
        if (s == SEEDS.first()) shown[name] = w
    }
    curves[name] = cumulative.map { it / population }
    println(
        "%-7s arrived %.3f of %d   mean travel %.1f"
            .format(
                name,
                cumulative.last() / population,
                population,
                travel / population,
            ),
    )

println("control that never left home would mean nothing.")

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"cling_and_climb","code":"/*
Two local drives that know about the environment, in the same weighted-blend idiom as
separate/align/cohere.

  cling(distance, clockwise) — follow the nearest wall at a chosen standoff. Tangential motion
  plus a radial correction, which is exactly what orbit() is; the difference is that the thing
  being orbited is read off the geometry rather than passed in.

  gradient(field, towards) — climb (or descend) a scalar field by central difference. Taxis:
  chemotaxis, phototaxis, whichever the field means. It finds a LOCAL maximum and has nothing
  to say about the global one, which is why two lamps split a population rather than gathering
  it — that is the correct behaviour, not a weight to tune away.
*/

val w = ScriptWorld(width = 200.0, height = 200.0, seed = 11L, wrap = false)
w.addDisc(62.0, 130.0, 26.0, segments = 28, name = "pillar")
w.addRect(120.0, 40.0, 50.0, 34.0, name = "block")

val lamps = pointSourceField(
    150.0,
    160.0,
    1.0,
    45.0,
    40.0,
    1.0,
    falloff = 26.0,
)

// Six clingers round the pillar, alternating direction — a population that all clings the same
// way never meets itself coming back.
repeat(6) { i ->
    val a = 2.0 * Math.PI * i / 6.0
    w.spawn(
        62.0 + Math.cos(a) * 36.0,
        130.0 + Math.sin(a) * 36.0,
        maxSpeed = 26.0,
        radius = 1.0,
        tag = "cling",
    ) {
        moveFor(12.0, 26.0) { cling(distance = 3.0, clockwise = self.id % 2 == 0) }
    }
}

/*
Nine climbers on a grid centred between the two lamps, with the block in the way of one of
them. Centred deliberately: start them nearer one lamp and "they split" is a claim about the
starting positions rather than about the sensing.
*/
repeat(9) { i ->
    val x = 78.0 + (i % 3) * 22.0
    val y = 78.0 + (i / 3) * 22.0
    w.spawn(x, y, maxSpeed = 18.0, radius = 1.0, tag = "climb") {
        moveFor(12.0, 18.0) {
            gradient(lamps, towards = true, probe = 2.0)
            avoidWalls(clearance = 3.0, weight = 0.5)
            separate(range = 5.0, weight = 0.4)
        }
    }
}

w.run(720)

val clingers = w.living.filter { it.tag == "cling" }
val climbers = w.living.filter { it.tag == "climb" }
fun near(a: ScriptActor, x: Double, y: Double) = Math.hypot(a.position.x - x, a.position.y - y) < 10.0

println(
    "cling  : mean distance to the nearest wall %.2f (asked for radius 1.0 + 3.0 = 4.0)"
        .format(
            clingers.map { w.wallField.distanceTo(it.position.x, it.position.y) }.average(),
        ),
)
println(
    "climb  : mean field value %.3f"
        .format(
            climbers.map { lamps.at(it.position.x, it.position.y) }.average(),
        ),
)

            climbers.count { near(it, 45.0, 40.0) },
            climbers.count { !near(it, 150.0, 160.0) && !near(it, 45.0, 40.0) },

)

What refuses. The function workbench's channels are fn(0.0..3600.0, name) { seconds -> ... }
lambdas: one opaque node each, so there is nothing for an interval walk to read. It refuses by
name rather than guess.
*/
val lambdaChannel = with(Functions) { fn(0.0..3600.0, "x") { t -> 0.45 + 0.2 * kotlin.math.sin(t) } }
val refused = lambdaChannel.enclose(0.0, 3600.0)

// The workbench's claim that an event holds exactly 1 for 30 seconds, rebuilt from formula ops:
// rise 185..285, hold to 315, fall to 415, over the moving background.
val held = with(Functions) {
    val one = c(1.0, Functions.Domain.ALL)
    val background = sin(1.0 / 40.0, amplitude = 0.2, offset = 0.45)
    val envelope =
        smoothStep(185.0, 285.0, Functions.Domain.ALL) * (one - smoothStep(315.0, 415.0, Functions.Domain.ALL))

A crescendo read by cutting it. A vertical line at a beat crosses the hairpin's two sides,
and the gap between the crossings is how loud it is: nothing at the point, most at the mouth.
Run this to draw one; then draw your own in the frame with the pen (Alt+D, then P) and this
box reads everything in the frame again. Two hairpins, or a diminuendo, read the same way.
*/
notation("hairpin") {
    frame("dynamics", 100, 1060, 800, 200)
    val hand = { i: Int -> 2.5 * sin(i * 2.3) + 1.5 * sin(i * 0.7) } // a hand is not a ruler
    val hairpin =
        (0..60).map { i ->
            val k = if (i <= 30) i else 60 - i // out along the top, back along the bottom
            val side = if (i <= 30) -1 else 1
            vec(860 - k * 23.0, 1160 + side * (75 - k * 2.5) + hand(i))
        }
    stroke(hairpin, name = "hairpin", stroke = "#e03131")
}
val dynamics = notation.space("dynamics", x = 0.0..8.0, y = 0.0..1.0)
val markings = ["niente", "pp", "p", "mp", "mf", "f", "ff"]
fun read() =
    (0..7).forEach { beat ->
        val ys = dynamics.vertical(beat.toDouble()).filter { !it.isSpan }.map { it.value }
        val gap = if (ys.size >= 2) ys.max() - ys.min() else 0.0
        println("beat $beat: %.2f %s".format(gap, markings[(gap / 0.75 * 6).roundToInt().coerceIn(0, 6)]))
    }

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"lambda_oracle","code":"/*
The whole corpus against the oracle, and then against four schedulers. This is the box that says
whether any of the rest is true: `readback(reduce(compile(t)))` against an ordinary
capture-avoiding normal-order evaluator, for every named term, printed rather than summarised.
*/

val corpus = LambdaTerms.corpus()
val orders = [
    ActivationOrder.FIRST_FOUND,
    ActivationOrder.LEFTMOST_BY_ID,
    ActivationOrder.RIGHTMOST_BY_ID,
    ActivationOrder.HIGHEST_PAIR_ENERGY,
]
println("${corpus.size} named closed terms, ${orders.size} schedulers")
println()

println("                        steps  fans  agents  normal form")
var netTotal = 0
val disagreed = mutableListOf<String>()
val notConfluent = mutableListOf<String>()

corpus.forEach { (name, source) ->
    val term = LambdaTerms.parse(source)
    val oracleKey = LambdaTerms.deBruijnKey(LambdaTerms.referenceNormalOrder(term))
    val keys = orders.associateWith { LambdaTerms.deBruijnKey(LambdaTerms.normalise(term, order = it).result) }
    val run = LambdaTerms.normalise(term)
    netTotal += run.steps
    if (keys.getValue(ActivationOrder.FIRST_FOUND) != oracleKey) disagreed += name
    if (keys.values.toSet().size != 1) notConfluent += name
    println(
        name.padEnd(22) + "%6d %5d %7d".format(run.steps, run.fans, run.remainingNodes) + "  " + run.printed.take(46),
    )
}

println()
println(
    "agreed with the oracle : ${corpus.size - disagreed.size} of ${corpus.size}" +
        if (disagreed.isEmpty()) "" else "   DISAGREED: $disagreed",
)
println(
    "confluent across ${orders.size} schedulers: ${corpus.size - notConfluent.size} of ${corpus.size}" +
        if (notConfluent.isEmpty()) "" else "   NOT CONFLUENT: $notConfluent",
)
println("net reactions          : $netTotal over ${corpus.size} terms at FIRST_FOUND")

/*
Two things that number is not. It is not comparable to a β-step count — a net reaction is any rule
firing, β or duplication or erasure or a fan meeting, so the two are different units. And it is not
the word "optimal": there are no brackets and no croissants here, so the sharing is correct but
nothing bounds how many times a fan may be copied.
*/

println("and the pieces on their own:")
println(
    "  parse -> format round-trips exactly: " +
        corpus.values.all { LambdaTerms.parse(LambdaTerms.format(LambdaTerms.parse(it))) == LambdaTerms.parse(it) },
)
println(
    "  every corpus term is closed: " +
        corpus.values.all { LambdaTerms.freeVariablesOf(LambdaTerms.parse(it)).isEmpty() },
)
println("  de Bruijn key of Church two: " + LambdaTerms.deBruijnKey(LambdaTerms.parse("\\f x. f (f x)")))
println(
    "  substitution avoids capture: " +
        LambdaTerms.format(LambdaTerms.substitute(LambdaTerms.parse("\\y. x y"), "x", LambdaTerms.parse("y"))),
)

/*

    println(

                m.triangleCount,
                m.signedVolume(),

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"condense_invents_nothing","code":"import kotlin.random.Random

/*
2 - Invent nothing.

The failure mode of a description-length search is naming a figure that is one step away
from the rhythm in front of it. This box runs that check live, on masks with no structure
put into them.

POKE THIS: change `seed`, or `density` (one step in N is on), or `trials`. The count of
wrong namings has to stay 0 whatever you set, because every mask that came back as a
whole-span figure is recomputed here from bjorklund / kolakoskiMask and compared.
*/
val seed = 20260910
val density = 3
val trials = 300

val random = Random(seed)
val euclidean = Regex("""^x\((\d+),(\d+)(?:,(\d+))?\)$""")
val kolakoskian = Regex("""^x\(([kg])(\d+)(?:,(\d+))?\)$""")

var named = 0
var wrong = 0
val ratios = mutableListOf<Double>()

repeat(trials) {
    val mask = List(16) { random.nextInt(density) == 0 }
    val condensed = patCondense(mask)
    ratios += condensed.compression
    euclidean.matchEntire(condensed.notation)?.let { m ->
        named++
        val pulses = m.groupValues[1].toInt()
        val steps = m.groupValues[2].toInt()
        val offset = m.groupValues[3].ifEmpty { "0" }.toInt()
        val figure = List(steps) { i -> bjorklund(pulses, steps)[((i + offset) % steps + steps) % steps] }
        if (figure != mask) wrong++
    }
    kolakoskian.matchEntire(condensed.notation)?.let { m ->
        named++
        val reading = if (m.groupValues[1] == "k") KolakoskiReading.RUNS else KolakoskiReading.GAPS
        val steps = m.groupValues[2].toInt()
        val offset = m.groupValues[3].ifEmpty { "0" }.toInt()
        if (kolakoskiMask(steps, reading, rotation = -offset) != mask) wrong++
    }
}

val median = ratios.sorted()[ratios.size / 2]
val structured = patCondense(kolakoskiMask(16)).compression

markdown(
    "main",
    """
    ### $trials random 16-step masks, seed $seed, one step in $density on

    | | |
    |---|---|
    | read as a single whole-span figure | **$named** |
    | of those, wrong | **$wrong** |
    | median compression | ${"%.3f".format(median)} |
    | the same number for `kolakoskiMask(16)` | ${"%.3f".format(structured)} |

    Noise compresses about ${"%.1f".format(median / structured)} times worse than the figure
    it is up against. That separation is the claim. If random masks compressed as well as
    structured ones, the search would be finding figures in nothing.

    None of this rests on the search's own opinion of itself: every string it returned was
    re-parsed and re-played before it was accepted, and the namings above are recomputed from
    the generators rather than read off the label.
    """
        .trimIndent(),
)

val hole = 0.45f

/*
A single square face, built by hand, optionally with one inner ring. This is the whole of
the hole API from a caller's side: record the ring's edges as incidences of the same face,
then declare the ring with addFaceHole. Winding is a convention — outer counter-clockwise
about the normal, inner clockwise — and nothing downstream leans on it, because the
tessellator decides which ring is the outer one geometrically.
*/
fun plate(withRing: Boolean): PolyhedralObject {
    val outer = [Vec3(-1f, -1f, 0f), Vec3(1f, -1f, 0f), Vec3(1f, 1f, 0f), Vec3(-1f, 1f, 0f)]
    val inner = [
        Vec3(-hole, -hole, 0f),
        Vec3(-hole, hole, 0f),
        Vec3(hole, hole, 0f),
        Vec3(hole, -hole, 0f),
    ]
    /*
    buildList, not `outer + inner`: a box has afield.geometry.path in scope, where
    `List<Vec3> + List<Vec3>` is element-wise vector addition and returns four points,
    not eight.
    */
    val points = buildList {
        addAll(outer)
        if (withRing) addAll(inner)
    }
    val rings = if (withRing) [[0, 1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6, 7]] else [[0, 1, 2, 3]]

    val builder = PolytopeTopologyBuilder(rank = 3)
    val vertices = points.map { builder.addElement(0) }
    val face = builder.addElement(2)
    for (ring in rings) for (i in ring.indices) {
        val edge = builder.addElement(1)
        builder.addIncidence(vertices[ring[i]], edge)
        builder.addIncidence(vertices[ring[(i + 1) % ring.size]], edge)
        builder.addIncidence(edge, face)
    }
    builder.setFaceCycle(face, rings.first().map { vertices[it] })
    rings.drop(1).forEach { ring -> builder.addFaceHole(face, ring.map { vertices[it] }) }
    builder.addIncidence(face, builder.addElement(3))
    return PolyhedralObject(builder.buildValidated(), Realization3(points))
}

cullBackFaces, deliberately: a rim triangle wound the wrong way would be *missing* here
exactly as it would be missing on a GPU, so this picture is a winding test as well as a
hole test. The wireframe is on so the eight rim triangles can be counted.

    yawDegrees = 0.0,

        val mesh = object3.toTriMesh()

                    " · ${mesh.triangleCount} triangles" +
                    " · area ${"%.3f".format(4.0 - if (withRing) 4.0 * hole * hole else 0.0)}",

    right: the identical outline with the ring dropped, ${plate(false).toTriMesh().triangleCount} triangles
    the filled area differs by exactly the ring: ${4.0 * hole * hole}

// Four seconds of 29.97 drop-frame LTC across the one-minute boundary.
val start = Timecode.parse("00:00:58;00")
val ltc = LtcEncoder.render(start, 4.0, sampleRate = 48000)

// Play it back badly: quiet, offset, noisy, and speeding up from 0.9x to 1.1x.
val rng = java.util.Random(1)
val played = ArrayList<Float>()
var p = 0.0
while (p < ltc.size - 1) {
    val k = p.toInt()
    val v = ltc[k] + (ltc[k + 1] - ltc[k]) * (p - k).toFloat()
    played += v * 0.1f + 0.2f + rng.nextGaussian().toFloat() * 0.01f
    p += 0.9 + 0.2 * p / ltc.size
}

val frames = LtcDecoder(48000, TimecodeRate.FPS_2997_DF).decodeAll(played.toFloatArray())

// Decoded frame number against playback time, and the speed the decoder measured.
val w = 640.0
val h = 220.0
val tMax = played.size / 48000.0
val fMax = frames.maxOf { it.timecode - start }.toDouble()
val pts = frames.joinToString(" ") {
    "%.1f,%.1f".format(it.sampleStart / 48000 / tMax * w, h - (it.timecode - start) / fMax * h)

val spd =

import afield.lang.solidsl.*

/*
---- a part that is half CSG and half field -------------------------------------------
A plate you could machine, unioned with a blob you could not: the fillet where the ball
meets the post lies on NEITHER of them, so no sequence of unions, intersections and
differences can produce it. The exact lowering says so instead of guessing.
*/
val fillet = 0.28

val machinable =
    cuboid(3.2, 3.2, 0.5) -
        unionOf(
            [-1.1 to -1.1, 1.1 to -1.1, -1.1 to 1.1, 1.1 to 1.1].map { (x, y) ->
                cylinder(2.0, 0.22, segments = 128).at(x, y, 0.0)
            },
        )
val organic = smoothUnion(
    sphere(0.62, segments = 128).at(0.0, 0.0, 0.95),
    cylinder(1.6, 0.28, segments = 128).at(0.0, 0.0, 0.45),
    k = fillet,
)
val part = machinable + organic

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

run {
    println("---- what this expression refuses, and why ----")
    part.allRefusals().forEach {
        println("  ${it.node}")
        println("    ${it.why}")
        println("    closable: ${it.closable}${if (it.missing.isNotBlank()) " — needs ${it.missing}" else ""}")
    }
    if (part.allRefusals().isEmpty()) println("  (nothing — every node has an exact CSG form)")
    println()

    // The catalogue, and why the last two refusals are a different kind from the first two.
    println("The catalogue, in full — try each of these:")
    listOf<Pair<String, SolidExpr>>(
            "smoothUnion(a, b, k)" to smoothUnion(sphere(1.0), cuboid(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), k = 0.2),
            "gyroid()" to gyroid(),
            "sphere(1).rounded(0.1)" to sphere(1.0).rounded(0.1),
            "sphere(1).shelled(0.05)" to sphere(1.0).shelled(0.05),
        )
        .forEach { (label, e) ->
            println("  %-24s %s".format(label, e.exactRefusal()!!.why.take(96) + "…"))
        }
    println()
    println("The last two are the interesting ones. They are NOT 'we did not get to it': an")
    println("exact-looking answer is available — Minkowski sum with a sphere — and it is the")
    println("WRONG answer, systematically, by up to that sphere's sagitta, in a direction that")
    println("does not shrink as the march refines. Filing that beside a smooth blend would")
    println("flatten a real distinction, so the reason says which kind it is.")
    println()

    if (!ManifoldLibrary.isAvailable) {
        println(ManifoldLibrary.describe())
        return@run
    }

    /*
    ---- the hybrid: the level set applied at the SMALLEST subtree that needs it -----------
    A naive fallback asks "does the whole tree lower exactly?" and marches everything if the
    answer is no — so one smooth blend anywhere costs a hundred-thousand-triangle
    approximation of a plate that was perfectly exact. This walks down instead.
    */
    val q = SolidQuality(segments = 128, edgeLengthFraction = 1.0 / 90.0)
    val build = part.buildSolid(q)
    println("---- the hybrid build ----")
    println(build.report())
    println()

    // What the naive version would have cost: one level set over the whole part, same edge length.
    val raw = part.bounds()!!
    val edge = maxOf(raw.size.x, raw.size.y, raw.size.z) / 90.0
    val naive =
        afield.geometry.solid.manifold.Solid.levelSet(raw.expandedBy(2.0 * edge), edge) { x, y, z ->
            part.toLevelSetField().at(x, y, z)
        }
    println("hybrid  ${build.solid.triangleCount} triangles")
    println("naive   ${naive.triangleCount} triangles for the same shape at the same edge length")
    println(
        "        — ${"%.2f".format(naive.triangleCount.toDouble() / build.solid.triangleCount)}x, and " +
            "the plate's six faces stay six faces",
    )
    println()

    val mesh = build.solid.toTriMesh()
    println("Field's own topology, sharing nothing with Manifold: watertight ${mesh.isWatertight()}")
    println("status ${build.solid.status} — guaranteed closed however the field behaved")

    showMesh(
        build.solid.toTriMesh(normals = true),
        channel = "hybrid",
        title = "exact where it can be, marched where it cannot",
        caption =
            "${build.solid.triangleCount} triangles · the plate and its four bores are exact CSG; " +
                "only the blended post was marched · the whole thing is still one guaranteed-closed solid",
        view = MeshView(yawDegrees = 36.0, pitchDegrees = 22.0, width = 720, height = 470),
    )

    build.close()

// Somebody hands you a bag of points with a signed distance at each. What shape is it?

val body = cuboid(1.0, 1.0, 0.4) - cylinder(1.2, 0.3).at(0.3, 0.0, 0.0)

differentiable form, because AD is closed over everything Field3 uses. So the refusals

                param("r", "Difference/0/Cuboid.y")
            },
        "two names for one number" to
            body.parameterize {
                param("a", "Difference/0/Cuboid.x")
                param("b", "Difference/0/Cuboid.x")
            },
        "tied slots with different seeds" to body.parameterize { param("size") { it.node == "Cuboid" } },
        "a Scale factor at zero" to
            sphere(0.5).sized(1.0, 1.0, 1.0).parameterize { param("s", "Scale.x", seed = 1e-9) },
        "a blend radius at zero" to
            smoothUnion(sphere(0.4), sphere(0.4).at(0.5, 0.0, 0.0), 0.2).parameterize {
                param("k", "SmoothUnion.k", seed = 0.0)
            },
    )

        println("  $what:")
        println("    ${l.refusalOrNull()}")
    }
println()
println("A SolidLowering.Refused rather than a thrown exception, for SolidExact.kt's own")
println("reason: a null invites a caller to substitute something plausible, and an exception")
println("loses the reason at the first runCatching. A mis-bound parameter is exactly the")
println("failure that presents as 'the optimiser ran and nothing happened'.")
println()

/*
---- and now the failure mode that is NOT a refusal -----------------------------------
A parameter can be perfectly legal and still have a gradient of exactly zero, which
presents as a CONVERGED optimisation. This is the thing to know about inverse design.
*/
val outer = sphere(1.0)
val inner = sphere(0.25) // entirely swallowed by `outer`
val samples = outer.sampleField(count = 800, seed = 3)

fun deadUnder(expr: SolidExpr, path: String): SolidFit {
    val t = expr.parameterize { param("inner", path) }.orThrow()
    return t.fitParameters(samples, doubleArrayOf(0.25), SolidFitOptions(iterations = 1))
}

println("---- a swallowed child, under two kinds of union ----")
val hard = deadUnder(unionOf([outer, inner]), "Union/1/Sphere.radius")
val soft = deadUnder(smoothUnion(outer, inner, 0.9), "SmoothUnion/b/Sphere.radius")
println("  hard Union      dead: ${hard.deadParameters}")
println("  smoothUnion     dead: ${soft.deadParameters}")

println("that is nowhere nearest receives exactly 0.0 from every sample, and a descent on")
println("it reports convergence immediately, because the gradient really is zero.")

println("of the seam contributes. That is the inversion this reading turns on: SmoothUnion")
println("and SmoothDifference are the two nodes the EXACT lowering refuses outright, and")
println("they are the two this one is best at. If a shape is going to be fitted, those are")

cell per site, the triangulation joins two sites exactly when their cells share an edge.
vec2VoronoiDualGraph is literally one line in the source that returns vec2DelaunayGraph.
*/

val sites =
    (0 until 54).map { i ->
        vec((i % 9) * 44.0 + rng.nextDouble() * 22.0, (i / 9) * 44.0 + rng.nextDouble() * 22.0)
    }

val triangles = vec2DelaunayTriangles(sites)
val voronoi = vec2VoronoiDiagram(sites)
val hull = vec2ConvexHull(sites)

/*
A planar triangulation of n sites with h on its convex hull has 2n-2-h triangles
and 3n-3-h edges. These count checks do not establish valid incidences, a noncrossing
embedding or Delaunay legality. The dual equality below checks the shared graph API.
*/
val n = sites.size
val h = hull.hullIndices.size
println("sites $n, hull $h")
println("triangles ${triangles.size}  expected 2n-2-h = ${2 * n - 2 - h}")
println("edges     ${delaunay.edges.size}  expected 3n-3-h = ${3 * n - 3 - h}")
println("dual == delaunay: ${vec2VoronoiDualGraph(sites).edges.toSet() == delaunay.edges.toSet()}")

/*
The cells of the h hull sites are UNBOUNDED, and JTS hands them back clipped to a
generous envelope rather than to anything you asked for. Print how far it reaches: fit a
figure to that and the diagram collapses into a speck, which is why showPlaneGrid takes
an explicit window and clips whatever falls outside it.

println()
println("site  x range %.1f .. %.1f".format(sites.minOf { it.x }, sites.maxOf { it.x }))

    "cell  x range %.1f .. %.1f   <- JTS's clip envelope"
        .format(
            allV.minOf { it.x },
            allV.maxOf { it.x },

)

    sites.minOf { it.x.toDouble() } - 18.0,
    sites.minOf { it.y.toDouble() } - 18.0,
    sites.maxOf { it.x.toDouble() } - sites.minOf { it.x.toDouble() } + 36.0,
    sites.maxOf { it.y.toDouble() } - sites.minOf { it.y.toDouble() } + 36.0,

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"spatial_apollonius","code":"/*
CircularDirichlet minimises |x - p|^2 / w^2 — the multiplicatively weighted, or
Apollonius, diagram. Setting two sites' scores equal and clearing denominators gives the
equation of a CIRCLE, which degenerates to a line only when the weights match. So a cell
here is not a polygon: its boundary is made of ArcPieces and LinePieces.
*/
val positions = [
    vec(0.0, 0.0),
    vec(2.2, 0.3),
    vec(0.9, 2.0),
    vec(-1.4, 1.1),
    vec(1.1, -1.6),
]
val clip = CircularDirichlet.Aabb(vec(-3.4, -3.4), vec(4.6, 4.6))

fun diagramOf(weights: List<Double>) =
    CircularDirichlet.build(positions.mapIndexed { i, p -> vec(p.x, p.y, weights[i]) })

val equal = diagramOf(List(5) { 1.0 })
val mixed = diagramOf([1.0, 1.35, 0.8, 1.1, 1.6])
val swallowed = diagramOf([1.0, 2.6, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0])

fun arcs(d: CircularDirichlet.Diagram) = d.cells.sumOf { c -> c.pieces.count { it is CircularDirichlet.ArcPiece } }
fun straights(d: CircularDirichlet.Diagram) =
    d.cells.sumOf { c -> c.pieces.count { it is CircularDirichlet.LinePiece } }
fun fullCircles(d: CircularDirichlet.Diagram) =
    d.cells.sumOf { c ->
        c.pieces.count { it is CircularDirichlet.ArcPiece && it.sweepAngle > 6.283 }
    }
fun enclosed(d: CircularDirichlet.Diagram) =
    d.cells.count { c ->
        c.pieces.size == 1 && (c.pieces[0] as? CircularDirichlet.ArcPiece)?.let { it.sweepAngle > 6.283 } == true
    }

// All-or-nothing, because the piece type is decided by an exact equality of weights.
println("equal weights : ${straights(equal)} straight, ${arcs(equal)} arcs")
println("mixed weights : ${straights(mixed)} straight, ${arcs(mixed)} arcs")
println("one at 2.6    : ${fullCircles(swallowed)} full-circle pieces, ${enclosed(swallowed)} cells wholly enclosed")

// Every boundary sample is a score tie between its two sites, and no third site beats it.
fun score(s: Vec3, p: Vec2) =
    ((p.x - s.x) * (p.x - s.x) + (p.y - s.y) * (p.y - s.y)).toDouble() / (s.z * s.z).toDouble()
val sites = positions.mapIndexed { i, p -> vec(p.x, p.y, [1.0, 1.35, 0.8, 1.1, 1.6][i]) }
var worstTie = 0.0
mixed.cells.forEach { cell ->
    cell.pieces.forEach { piece ->
        val p = piece.samplePoint()
        val own = score(sites[cell.siteIndex], p)
        val other = score(sites[piece.neighborSite], p)
        worstTie = maxOf(worstTie, kotlin.math.abs(own - other) / maxOf(1.0, own))
    }
}
println()
println("worst relative score gap across every boundary sample: %.3e".format(worstTie))

val palette = okhslSet(5, saturation = 0.8, lightness = 0.66)
val cloud = pointCloudFLine(positions, color = vec(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.95), pointSize = 1.6)
fun panel(d: CircularDirichlet.Diagram) =
    d.toFLines(clip = clip, maxChordError = 0.01f, palette = palette, thickness = 1.6) + cloud

showPlaneGrid(
    "equal weights — a plain Voronoi diagram\n${straights(equal)} straight bisectors, ${arcs(equal)} arcs" to
        panel(equal),
    "weights 1.0 / 1.35 / 0.8 / 1.1 / 1.6\n${arcs(mixed)} arcs, ${straights(mixed)} straight" to panel(mixed),
    "one site at weight 2.6\n${fullCircles(swallowed)} complete circles, ${enclosed(swallowed)} cells enclosed" to
        panel(swallowed),
    columns = 2,
    cellWidth = 430,
    cellHeight = 280,
)

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"spatial_contours","code":"/*
A Voronoi diagram IS the set of ties in argmin |x - p_i|, so contouring the gap between
the nearest and the second nearest site recovers it from a completely different
algorithm. Except at exactly zero — see below.
*/
val sites = [
    vec(-1.6, -0.9),
    vec(1.4, -1.2),
    vec(2.0, 1.1),
    vec(-0.2, 1.7),
    vec(-2.1, 0.9),
    vec(0.4, -0.1),
]
val gap: ScalarField2D = { x, y ->
    val d = sites.map { s -> kotlin.math.hypot(x - s.x, y - s.y) }.sorted()
    d[1] - d[0]
}

/*
This field is NON-NEGATIVE: it touches zero on the seams and is positive everywhere
else. Marching squares finds SIGN CHANGES, so iso 0.0 finds nothing at all, and that is
the right answer rather than a bug. Every min-of-distances or absolute-value field
behaves this way.
*/
val atZero = generateIsoContours(gap, -3.4, 3.4, -2.9, 2.9, 120, 120, 0.0)
var lo = Double.MAX_VALUE
var hi = -Double.MAX_VALUE
for (i in 0..120) for (j in 0..120) {
    val v = gap(-3.4 + i * 6.8 / 120.0, -2.9 + j * 5.8 / 120.0)
    if (v < lo) lo = v
    if (v > hi) hi = v
}
println("field range %.3e .. %.4f  (never negative)".format(lo, hi))
println("iso 0.0 exactly -> ${atZero.size} contours")

val levels = [0.05, 0.35, 0.8, 1.4]
val byLevel = levels.map { iso -> iso to generateIsoContours(gap, -3.4, 3.4, -2.9, 2.9, 120, 120, iso) }
byLevel.forEach { (iso, cs) ->
    println("iso %.2f -> %2d contours, %4d points".format(iso, cs.size, cs.sumOf { it.size }))
}

/*
A completely different use of the same machinery: pointEdgeScalarField2D turns an FLine
into a signed field whose zero set is a tube around it, so contouring at 0.0 outlines a
stroke and a negative iso fattens it.
*/
val stroke = fline {
    moveTo(-2.4, 1.2)
    cubicTo(-1.0, -2.2, 1.2, 2.4, 2.6, -1.0)
}
val outline = generateSmoothIsoContours(stroke, radius = 0.55, spatialStep = 0.05)
val fat = generateSmoothIsoContours(stroke, radius = 0.55, spatialStep = 0.05, iso = -0.28)
println()
println("tube outlines: ${outline.size} at radius 0.55, ${fat.size} at 0.83")

fun contourLines(contours: List<List<Vec2>>, color: Vec4, thickness: Double) =
    contours
        .filter { it.size >= 2 }
        .map { c ->
            polylineFrom(c, 0, closed = isoContourClosed(c, -3.4, 3.4, -2.9, 2.9, boundaryEpsilon = 0.05)).also {
                it.color = color
                it.thickness = thickness

val ramp = okhslSet(levels.size, saturation = 0.82, lightness = 0.66, startHue = 0.55f)
val stacked =

        contourLines(contours, ramp[i], 1.5 - i * 0.15)

                    f.thickness = 1.6

    cellWidth = 430,

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"spatial_marching","code":"// Marching squares has exactly two decisions in it, and both are places where a plausible
// implementation is quietly wrong. Each input below has an answer you already know.
val plane: ScalarField2D = { x, _ -> x }
val circle: ScalarField2D = { x, y -> kotlin.math.hypot(x, y) - 1.0 }
val saddle: ScalarField2D = { x, y -> x * y }

/*
1. A sample EXACTLY at iso. With a symmetric strict test such a sample is neither inside
nor outside and the crossing on every edge out of that corner is suppressed. f(x,y) = x
at iso 0 on an even grid used to return an empty list; the unit circle over [-2,2] at
nx = 16 came back severed into four arcs at the points where it passes through a corner.
The convention now is the one marchingCubes uses: inside iff strictly BELOW iso.
*/
val planeContours = generateIsoContours(plane, -1.0, 1.0, -1.0, 1.0, 4, 4, 0.0)
val aligned = generateIsoContours(circle, -2.0, 2.0, -2.0, 2.0, 16, 16, 0.0)
println("f(x,y) = x at iso 0, nx = 4 -> ${planeContours.size} contour of ${planeContours.sumOf { it.size }} points")
println("unit circle at nx = 16      -> ${aligned.size} loop of ${aligned[0].size} points")

fun perimeter(loop: List<Vec2>): Double {
    var total = 0.0
    for (i in loop.indices) {
        val a = loop[i]
        val b = loop[(i + 1) % loop.size]
        total += kotlin.math.hypot((a.x - b.x).toDouble(), (a.y - b.y).toDouble())
    }
    return total
}
println("   perimeter %.4f against 2pi = %.4f".format(perimeter(aligned[0]), 2 * PI))

/*
2. The saddle cell. Four corners alternating inside/outside give four crossings and two
ways to pair them, and the two choices give different topology — so an arbitrary choice
lets neighbouring cells disagree and the contour tears. The asymptotic decider settles it
from the cell's own four corner values, so two cells sharing an edge always agree.

f = x*y is the case where it has nothing to go on: the field is ITSELF bilinear, so the
cell's interpolant reproduces it and the saddle value is exactly iso. Both pairings are
then equally correct. Left to floating point that tie flips with resolution, so it is
broken deterministically towards the pre-decider pairing. Raise nx and watch the branch
lengths: they are not equal, and with this sampling window they are not meant to be.
*/
val branches = generateIsoContours(saddle, -1.05, 1.03, -1.02, 1.07, 8, 8, 0.0)
println()
println("f = x*y at iso 0 -> ${branches.size} branches of ${branches.map { it.size }.joinToString(" and ")} points")
println("   (a genuine tie: the saddle sits exactly on iso, so either pairing is correct)")

fun gridLines(x0: Double, x1: Double, y0: Double, y1: Double, nx: Int, ny: Int) = fline {
    grid(Rect(x0, y0, x1 - x0, y1 - y0), nx, ny)
    color = vec(0.34, 0.42, 0.54, 0.55)
    thickness = 0.8
}

    contours: List<List<Vec2>>,
    x0: Double,
    x1: Double,
    y0: Double,
    y1: Double,
    colors: List<Vec4>,
    eps: Double,

    polylineFrom(c, 0, closed = isoContourClosed(c, x0, x1, y0, y1, eps)).also {
        it.color = colors[i % colors.size]
        it.thickness = 2.2
        it.pointed = true
        it.pointSize = 1.1
    }

    vec(0.62, 0.92, 1.0, 0.95),
    vec(0.98, 0.55, 0.62, 0.95),

    cellWidth = 430,
    cellHeight = 280,

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"spatial_iso_sweep","code":"/*
The animated twin of "The two decisions inside marching squares". That box argues about a
single ambiguous cell; this one shows why the cell matters. Two Gaussian bumps, and the
iso level swept from 0.18 to 0.78 and back through the saddle between the peaks. Below
the saddle there is ONE contour around both peaks, above it there are TWO, one per peak,
and the changeover is a frame where the marcher's four corner values decide the topology.
Contours are coloured by index, so the merge reads as a colour vanishing.
*/
val field: ScalarField2D = { x, y ->
    exp(-((x - 1.4) * (x - 1.4) + y * y) / 1.2) + exp(-((x + 1.4) * (x + 1.4) + y * y) / 1.2)
}
val x0 = -3.2
val x1 = 3.2
val y0 = -1.9
val y1 = 1.9
val window = Rect(-3.0, -1.7, 6.0, 3.4) // fixed, or the loops never appear to shrink
val peakDots = pointCloudFLine(
    [vec(1.4, 0.0), vec(-1.4, 0.0)],
    color = vec(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.85),
    pointSize = 1.4,
)
val saddleDot = pointCloudFLine(
    [vec(0.0, 0.0)],
    color = vec(1.0, 0.72, 0.32, 0.98),
    pointSize = 1.9,
)
val byIndex = [vec(0.42, 0.80, 1.0, 0.95), vec(1.0, 0.45, 0.62, 0.95)]
val sweepSeconds = 8.0

// The saddle level is the field's own value at the col.
val saddle = field(0.0, 0.0)
println("saddle level %.3f — below it one contour, above it two".format(saddle))
val started = AnimationClock.nowSeconds()

// The line that turns elapsed time into the swept parameter, straddling the saddle.
fun isoAt(elapsed: Double): Double {
    val phase = (elapsed / sweepSeconds) % 1.0
    return 0.18 + 0.60 * (1.0 - abs(1.0 - 2.0 * phase))
}

animate {
    val iso = isoAt(AnimationClock.nowSeconds() - started)
    val contours = generateIsoContours(field, x0, x1, y0, y1, 100, 60, iso).filter { it.size >= 2 }
    val lines = contours.mapIndexed { i, c ->
        polylineFrom(c, 0, closed = isoContourClosed(c, x0, x1, y0, y1, boundaryEpsilon = 0.05)).also {
            it.color = byIndex[i % byIndex.size]
            it.thickness = 2.0

        title = "iso %.3f — %d contour(s)".format(iso, contours.size),
        caption =
            if (iso > saddle) "above the saddle %.3f — one loop per peak".format(saddle)
            else "below the saddle %.3f — one loop around both".format(saddle),
        width = 560,
        height = 320,
        window = window,
    )
}

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"three-inspector-wall","code":"/*
The three.js output area as an INSTRUMENT.

Run this box. A wall detail appears -- four skins and five conduit runs -- and
the viewer's toolbar has three things a 3D preview never had before:

  [ruler]    click it, then click two things in the scene. The CLOSEST APPROACH
             between them is drawn as a dimension, in millimetres. Not centroid
             to centroid: on a panel drawing those are different numbers, and
             only one of them is the one you would take to a saw. Click a third
             time to start over.

  [section]  turn it on and a second slider appears. The fills clip -- and the
             CUT is drawn over them in cyan, with a dot wherever a conduit
             crosses the plane. The status line, top right, reports the total
             length of the cut and where the plane sits. Hiding the front half
             shows you the inside of a shell; the cut line is the section.

  explode    drag it and the four skins come apart, spaced evenly by their
             ORDER through the wall rather than by how far apart they actually
             are -- 90, 50 and 12 mm, which under a distance-proportional
             explode would leave three of them in a clump. Drag it back to 0
             and the geometry is exactly what the server sent, bit for bit.

The two dimensions below are authored from Kotlin, so the figure carries them
from the moment it is drawn. `ThreeMeasureElement.face(line)` names a whole
panel; `.segment(...)` and `.point(...)` name the other two shapes a hit can
resolve to, which is not a coincidence -- a measurement you pick in the viewer
produces exactly these.
*/

fun skin(name: String, x: Double, c: Vec4) = fline {
    moveTo(x, 0.0, 0.0)
    lineTo(x, 1600.0, 0.0)
    lineTo(x, 1600.0, 1800.0)
    lineTo(x, 0.0, 1800.0)
    close()
    label = name
    filled = true
    stroked = true
    thickness = 1.4
    color = c
}

// x is the depth through the wall, in millimetres. 152 mm of build-up.
val wall = [
    skin("sheathing", 0.0, vec(0.36, 0.46, 0.58, 0.5)),
    skin("studs", 90.0, vec(0.85, 0.62, 0.32, 0.28)),
    skin("services", 140.0, vec(0.35, 0.72, 0.86, 0.28)),
    skin("lining", 152.0, vec(0.90, 0.92, 0.96, 0.4)),
]

val conduits =
    (0 until 5).map { i ->
        fline {
            val y = 200.0 + i * 320.0
            moveTo(120.0, y, 80.0)
            lineTo(120.0, y, 1720.0)
            label = "conduit $i"
            stroked = true
            thickness = 4.0
            color = vec(1.0, 0.45, 0.30, 1.0)
        }
    }

/*
`groupBy` decides what counts as one PART of the assembly. It defaults to the
FLine's label, which is why the five conduits fan out separately here; group
them together with `groupBy = { if (it.label?.startsWith("conduit") == true) "conduits" else it.label ?: "" }`.
*/
val view = threeInspect(
    wall + conduits,
    channel = "wall",
    height = 560,
    units = "mm",
    explode = ThreeExplode(mode = "axis", axis = floatArrayOf(1f, 0f, 0f), sliderMax = 1400.0),
    measurements = [
        // the build-up: 152 by construction, and the figure now says so
        ThreeMeasurement(
            ThreeMeasureElement.face(wall[0]),
            ThreeMeasureElement.face(wall[3]),
            "build-up ",
        ),
        // the clearance from a conduit to the inside of the lining: 152 - 120 = 32,
        // which is written down nowhere in the geometry
        ThreeMeasurement(
            ThreeMeasureElement.segment(120.0, 840.0, 80.0, 120.0, 840.0, 1720.0),
            ThreeMeasureElement.face(wall[3]),
            "clear ",
        ),
    ],
)

/*
And because the explosion is a PARAMETER rather than a literal you retype, the
box can drive it. Uncomment any of these and re-run -- no rebuild of the
geometry, just a new question:

view.explode(700.0)                                  // pull it apart
view.explodeAlong(0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 500.0)              // ...along z instead
view.section(0.0, 0.0, 1.0, fraction = 0.55)         // cut it
view.clearSection()
view.measureFaces(wall[1], wall[2], "cavity ")       // one more dimension
view.clearMeasurements()
*/

println("wall: ${view.inspector().groups.size} assembly groups, ${view.inspector().measurements.size} dimensions")
println("drag the explode slider; press the ruler and click two things")

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"typo_winding","code":"/*
Both cells below go through the identical filler at the identical fill rule. The only
difference is whether hole rings run the opposite way to their bowls. NON_ZERO fill —
which is what Skia and Java2D both do — cancels a +1 outer against a -1 hole and leaves a
counter; give it two rings wound the same way and it fills them solid.
*/
val face = typeface("SansSerif", 220.0)
val layout = layoutText("open", face)
val window = layout.bounds

val withConvention = rasterizeText(
    layout,
    900,
    460,
    window = window,
    fillRule = TextFillRule.NON_ZERO,
    rings = layout.toContours(honourHoles = true),
)
val withoutConvention = rasterizeText(
    layout,
    900,
    460,
    window = window,
    fillRule = TextFillRule.NON_ZERO,
    rings = layout.toContours(honourHoles = false),
)

/*
EVEN_ODD counts crossings and ignores their direction, so it depends on nesting parity
instead and fills the counters correctly either way. Two rules that agree on correct input
and disagree on broken input is a cross-check, which is why both are in the API.
*/
val evenOdd = rasterizeText(layout, 900, 460, window = window, fillRule = TextFillRule.EVEN_ODD)

var worst = 0.0
for (y in 0 until withConvention.height) for (x in 0 until withConvention.width) {
    worst = maxOf(worst, kotlin.math.abs(withConvention.at(x, y, 0) - evenOdd.at(x, y, 0)).toDouble())
}

showImgGrid(
    "NON_ZERO, convention on: counters are holes" to withConvention,
    "NON_ZERO, convention off: counters fill solid" to withoutConvention,
    "EVEN_ODD over the correct rings" to evenOdd,
    columns = 3,
    cellSide = 420,
)
println("ink with the convention  : ${"%.2f".format(100 * withConvention.inkFraction())}%")
println(
    "ink without it           : ${"%.2f".format(100 * withoutConvention.inkFraction())}%  <- the counters closed up",
)
println("worst NON_ZERO vs EVEN_ODD difference over the correct rings: $worst (0.0 means the two rules agree exactly)")
","parent":""}},{"tool":"RunBoxRequest","arguments":{"box":"typo_winding","timeoutSeconds":90.0}},{"final":"Made typo_winding from its transcript code and ran it."}]

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"typo_mesh","code":"/*
extrudeMesh and triangulatePolygon in mesh_generate.kt say outright that they cannot do
holes, and a letter is a ring SYSTEM. So toMesh triangulates the caps with FloatEarcut and
hole indices, and builds the walls from the same flattened vertices the caps used — which
is what makes the result watertight, and what makes genus a meaningful question about a
letter.
*/
val face = typeface("SansSerif", 170.0)
val o = layoutText("o", face).toMesh(depth = 46.0, centre = true)
val l = layoutText("l", face).toMesh(depth = 46.0, centre = true)
val word = layoutText("mesh", typeface("SansSerif", 130.0)).toMesh(depth = 36.0, centre = true)

// A 2D count against a 3D one. The hole count comes from ring nesting in the plane; the
// genus comes from counting the mesh's vertices, edges and faces.
for ((name, mesh, holes) in
    [
        Triple("o", o, layoutText("o", face).holeCount),
        Triple("l", l, layoutText("l", face).holeCount),
        Triple("mesh", word, layoutText("mesh", typeface("SansSerif", 130.0)).holeCount),
    ]) {
    println(
        "'$name': ${mesh.triangleCount} triangles, watertight ${mesh.isWatertight()}, " +
            "manifold ${mesh.isManifold()}, chi ${mesh.eulerCharacteristic()}, genus ${mesh.genus()} " +
            "(2D hole count $holes)",
    )
}

// A 2D area against a 3D volume: a shoelace sum times the depth, against the divergence
// theorem over the triangles. A dropped cap triangle or a wall wound the wrong way breaks it.
val flat = layoutText("o", face)
val expected = flat.glyphs.sumOf { it.glyph.inkArea } * 46.0
val measured = layoutText("o", face).toMesh(depth = 46.0, yUp = false).volume()
println(
    "'o': ink area x depth = ${"%.0f".format(expected)}, mesh volume ${"%.0f".format(measured)}, " +
        "relative difference ${"%.2e".format(kotlin.math.abs(expected - measured) / expected)}",
)

/*
Back-face culling is on in MeshView, so a wall wound inside out would be a MISSING wall
here rather than merely odd shading. No flatShaded() either: showMeshGrid computes
topology() on what you hand it and prints it in the caption, and flatShaded() un-welds
every triangle — so a flat-shaded copy would caption these as open, directly under a
title stating their genus. It is also unnecessary: the render path applies
shadedNormals to an unshaded mesh for you (mesh_field.kt:246).
*/
showMeshGrid(
    "o — genus ${o.genus()}" to o,
    "l — genus ${l.genus()}" to l,
    columns = 2,
    cellWidth = 400,
    view = MeshView(yawDegrees = 26.0, pitchDegrees = 16.0, distance = 3.2),
)
displayOpen("word")
showMesh(
    word,
    channel = "word",
    view = MeshView(yawDegrees = 22.0, pitchDegrees = 14.0, distance = 2.6, width = 820, height = 340),
    title = "extruded from the same contours the raster filled",
)

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"typo_sdf","code":"/*
toSdf builds a 2D signed-distance grid over the layout, samples it bilinearly and extrudes
it in z with the exact prism formula. Negative inside the ink, per mesh_sdf.kt's
convention. From there letters are just another ScalarField3D, which is the point.
*/
val layout = layoutText("SDF", typeface("SansSerif", 170.0))
val sdf = layout.toSdf(depth = 0.24, gridResolution = 340)
val grid = sdf.distanceField
println(
    "grid ${grid.nx}x${grid.ny} over ${"%.0f".format(grid.bounds.w)}x${"%.0f".format(grid.bounds.h)} units; " +
        "deepest inside the ink ${"%.1f".format(grid.deepestInside())} units",
)

val marched = sdf.march(resolution = 130)
println("marchingCubes: ${marched.triangleCount} triangles, genus ${marched.genus()}")

// And now the composition that having letters in this family buys you.
val melted = marchingCubes(sdfSmoothUnion(sdf.field, sdfSphere(0.6, vec(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)), 0.18), sdf.bounds, 130)
val hollow = marchingCubes(sdf.field.shell(0.02), sdf.bounds, 150)
val wrung = marchingCubes(sdf.field.twisted(0.5), sdf.bounds, 130)
println(
    "smooth union with a sphere: ${melted.triangleCount} triangles; " +
        "shelled: ${hollow.triangleCount}; twisted: ${wrung.triangleCount}",
)

displayOpen("sdf")
showImg(
    grid.toImg(),
    channel = "sdf",
    caption = "the 2D signed distance field — mid grey is the outline",
)
showMeshGrid(
    "marchingCubes on the letters" to marched,
    "sdfSmoothUnion with a sphere" to melted,
    "field.shell(0.02)" to hollow,
    "field.twisted(0.5)" to wrung,
    columns = 2,
    cellWidth = 400,
    view = MeshView(yawDegrees = 18.0, pitchDegrees = 12.0, distance = 2.6),
)

[{"tool":"NewBoxRequest","arguments":{"name":"typo_points","code":"/*
The last bridge is the plainest: even-by-arc-length samples along the outlines, which is
what every point-consuming family in the stdlib eats. Once a word is points, the
clusterers, the triangulators and the alife agents all work on letters.
*/
val layout = layoutText("field", typeface("SansSerif", 200.0))
val coarse = layout.samplePoints(spacing = 18.0)
val fine = layout.samplePoints(spacing = 4.5)
println(
    "spacing 18 -> ${coarse.size} points, spacing 4.5 -> ${fine.size} points " +
        "(${"%.2f".format(fine.size.toDouble() / coarse.size)}x for 4x finer)",
)

// Delaunay over the outline samples: the triangulation of a word.
val graph = vec2DelaunayGraph(coarse)
println("Delaunay over ${coarse.size} outline samples: ${graph.edges.size} edges")

// And k-medoids, which finds the strokes: six clusters over the same points, each medoid an
// actual sample rather than an average.
val km = vec2KMedoids(coarse, k = 6, options = KMedoidsOptions(randomSeed = 11L))
val layer = ClusterLayer("outline strokes", km.labels)
println(
    "k-medoids k=6: sizes ${km.labels.toList().groupingBy { it }.eachCount().values.sorted()}, " +
        "distortion ${"%.1f".format(km.distortion)}, converged ${km.converged}",
)

// Every panel shares one window, so the four views of the same word line up.
val window = layout.bounds
showPlaneGrid(
    "outline samples (${coarse.size} at spacing 18)" to [layout.toPointFLine(spacing = 18.0, pointSize = 1.1)],
    "Delaunay over those samples" to
        [graph.toFLine(coarse, thickness = 0.8), layout.toPointFLine(spacing = 18.0, pointSize = 0.9)],
    "k-medoids, k = 6" to layer.toFLines(coarse, centers = km.medoids, drawSpokes = false),
    "the outlines the samples came from" to layout.toFLines(thickness = 1.2),
    columns = 2,
    cellWidth = 400,
    cellHeight = 240,
    window = window,
)
